A stylishly quirky master of the cult film, director Joe Dante took a giant step forward into mainstream filmmaking with Gremlins, a savagely witty fairy tale and resounding boxoffice success. To an extent beyond that of any recent film, Gremlins relied almost as much on its variously conceived mechanical creatures as it did on its live performers. With contributions from Joe Dante, producer Michael Finnell and others, mogwai and gremlin creator Chris Walas unveils the story behind the year's most remarkable cinematic newcomers. Scaled, bat-eared creatures in microwave ovens pop wide open like rotten fruit. A midnight screening of Snow White literally brings down the house. Cooing, living balls of fur ride toy cars through the aisles of Montgomery Ward's, desperately trying to stop chainsaw wielding monsters less than two feet high. What is this? A nightmare? A put-on? A bad, bad joke? No. But then again, yes ... Gremlins is the story of a teenage boy whose cute, living Christmas present nearly leads to the destruction of his home town. The film, a second collaboration between executive producer Steven Spielberg and director Joe Dante - the "It's a Good Life" episode of the Twilight Zone movie being their first - is something of an apotheosis in Dante's career. Constantly fluctuating in tone between the hip and the horrible, from the silly to the sadistic, Gremlins is a live-action feature employing the hyperkinetic language of animated cartoons, not to mention a crateful of movie-ish in-jokes. It is also, even for Dante - already well-known for his use of high-tech makeup effects in The Howling and Twilight Zone - one of the most voluminous examples of the in-camera, shot-while-on-stage special effects films of all time. However, as with most other motion pictures, in the beginning was the word. In late 1981, while preparing the release of his 1982 smash hit E.T., Steven Spielberg received a first draft Gremlins script from a then unknown screenwriter named Chris Columbus. Although Columbus' agent had submitted the Gremlins piece as a writing sample, one not to be regarded as an actual polished work, Spielberg was nonetheless taken by the script. Subsequently, after viewing "Gizmo," a twenty-fiveminute short film Columbus had done while at New York University, Spielberg bought the Gremlins property. "Gremlins was impressive," Spielberg has said. "You can drop a stone into the black hole of Chris' imagination and never hear it hit bottom. But I'd never thought of directing Gremlins myself. I wanted to take a long vacation from anything with a wire trailing from its rear end that makes a creature smile when you pull it. Joe Dante seemed perfect for that job." Columbus' first draft focused on the relationship between young Billy Peltzer and his new pet, an adorable but strange creature called a mogwai, which - it is soon discovered - has the unfortunate habit of procreating asexually into a number of considerably less benign creatures that quickly overrun the mythical Anywhere U.S.A. town of Kingston Falls. "Originally." said Joe Dante, "the first draft Gremlins script was a pretty straightforward horror story, with little humor and a different set of characters - no Mrs. Deagle and no Futtermans. One sequence, though, that I am now a little sorry about being dropped from the first draft was when the kids go into a McDonald's and all the people have been eaten - but not the burgers." In spite of the horror - or perhaps because of it - certain aspects of Columbus' initial screenplay appealed to Dante. "One thing I liked about the first draft was that you really felt that the gremlins just did not think in human terms. They were crazy! As the script evolved, I also liked the idea that all the mechanical devices people depend on are turned against them - and the gremlins think that's just the funniest thing in the world." Despite everyone's enthusiasm for the project, a fully-approved shooting script was not to be until Columbus had passed eight additional drafts through his typewriter. Although Spielberg had purchased the property intending to become personally involved in its production, with the completion of E.T. came his commitment to Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, which of necessity precluded his direct day-to-day participation in Gremlins. Therefore, in conjunction with close associates Frank Marshall and Kathleen Kennedy, Spielberg opted instead for the role of executive producer. Selected as line producer for the project was Michael Finnell, who had served in like capacity on the Dante Twilight Zone episode. A fellow alumnus of the Roger Corman school of filmmaking, Finnell had worked with Dante in various capacities, including producer, on Hollywood Boulevard, Rock n' Roll High School and The Howling, as well as independently on such films as Airplane - where his role as miniature and optical effects supervisor earned him on-screen billing as 'Generally in Charge of Lots of Things.' But what of Gremlins? Why make such a film at all? The term 'gremlins' was popularized during World War II, when small creatures were blamed - particularly by airmen - for getting into machinery and causing breakdowns. Actually, though, the term predates that period. As early as World War I, flyers were already blaming the creatures for various problems. And perhaps it was no small coincidence that gremlins were also reputed to be the goblins which popped out of a bottle of Fremlins - the product of a brewery in Kent, England. Whatever the origin, the filmmakers were determined to take advantage of the gremlins legend. "We liked the idea of mischievous creatures whose idea of a good time is to louse things up and make things difficult for people," said Finnell, who received his second draft at about the same time Universal scuttled the 3-D remake of The Creature from the Black Lagoon he was to have coproduced with director Jack Arnold and executive producer John Landis. "I had been talking to Chris Walas about doing Creature's special makeup effects, so I sent Columbus' script up to him and asked, 'What do you think about this?' In 1975, Walas entered the film program at Los Angeles City College and, two years later, joined the Don Post Studios as a painter. After leaving Post and working on effects makeup for several television shows, Walas teamed up with Dante on Piranha - the director's second credit - on which he worked with the effects team. Since then, Walas has contributed makeup and other effects to such films as Scanners, Caveman, Dragonslayer, Raiders of the Lost Ark and Romancing the Stone. "Gremlins," said Walas, "seemed so intriguing a challenge that I snapped it right up. Very fortunately, for a project of this scope, Mike and Joe kept me involved in every step of the process, from the moment I received the second draft screenplay - which was in early 1982 - to the final cut. From the effects end, the scope of the picture was awesome. I turned pale when I read lines like: 'Hordes of gremlins - thousands and thousands of them - pour through the town.' And the creature nomenclature was a little confusing, too. In the script, they were just called mogwai all the way through. To keep things straight, we started calling the nice little furry ones mogwai and the mean nasty ones gremlins. In fact, to simplify it even further, our own crew got to calling the mogwai MGs and the gremlins GMs." Despite his initial apprehension at the effects-heavy aspects of Gremlins, the Marin County-based Walas agreed to participate of cremins, the eart in the project. "Steven's original idea for Gremlins was to do it as a very low-budget, non-union film at the Osmonds' studio in Utah. For varying reasons that didn't work out. One was that I didn't want to do it on location; and two, once we got Chris Walas involved, it became obvious that the special effects were going to be more expansive and the picture more expensive than Steven had hoped. We then all realized that we were going to need studio backing in order to make the film. Just exactly how Gremlins got to Warner Brothers I'm not really clear. I would imagine it had something to do with our doing Twilight Zone there. But even though Warners was interested in developing the picture, they were a little recalcitrant about putting out the money up front. We never really got a green light on Gremlins - more like yellow-green. It was okay to build the sets, but it wasn't okay to hire the cast. It was okay to hire this person, but not that person. Gremlins got its go-ahead in dribs and drabs. Once it finally did, though, Steven and I and Chris Columbus and Mike had changed the focus of the script, from being a 'B' horror movie into something different. Unfortunately, I can't tell you exactly what that 'different' is." "What really closed our deal with Warners," said Finnell, "was some test footage that we shot of one of Chris' first gremlins. The studio looked at that in January of '83 and thought: 'Well, these guys seem to be pretty serious. Let's do it.'" Due to the complexities of the project, the Gremlins preproduction phase was particularly lengthy. "Luckily," Finnell con-

tinued, "Joe and I had had some storyboarding experience with The Howling, so we decided to storyboard as many of the Gremlins effects sequences in advance as we could. In fact, we began boarding Gremlins while we were still shooting Twilight Zone, because there was no way Chris could even begin building certain puppets until he had storyboards. In some shots, we might need a gremlin from the waist up only, while in others there might be a full, free-standing creature in the frame. Each would be very different in terms of its construction. So everything was built to storyboard. Of course, we had a certain amount of flexibility to change these boards as we went along; but at least Chris had, in the beginning, a good firm idea of what we needed so he could go ahead and start building things." The first Gremlins storyboards were actually produced by Joe Dante, who had trained as a cartoonist early in life. (One especially telling panel featured a mogwai standing in a crate labeled 'One (1) Acme Mogwai - Made in Taiwan.') Dante was later superseded by storyboard artist David Negron, who illustrated the bulk of the picture during preproduction. Dick Lasley - a Poltergeist veteran - then joined the production, providing boards for the duration of the show and working closely with production designer James H. Spencer. At the same time Gremlins' action was being graphically laid out, Joe Dante was finding the relationship with his executive producer to be a pleasant one. "I had heard some rumors about the Spielberg/Hooper situation on Poltergeist," Dante commented, "and frankly I had some trepidation about it, because nobody wants to make a picture for someone who should really be making it himself. But my fears were groundless. Once we finally had the script honed down and Steven approved the two leads, he seemed much more involved in Indiana Jones. In fact, just before he left the U.S. to shoot Indiana, the last thing he said to me was: 'Go ahead. Make the picture. It's your picture. Don't even show it to me until you think it's finished.' Now, even Roger Corman never said that to me! And that's exactly what happened. Steven was on the set only once, for two days, when Harrison Ford hurt his back on Indy and they had to shut down for a couple of weeks. Other than that, Steven never even looked at the film until we had about a two-hour rough cut to show him." By now the Gremlins script had been made much more humorous, with a heavy peppering of Dante's trademark injokes. The character of the gremlins, too, had been softened, with their actions now motivated more out of an urge for dangerous fun than sheer hungry viciousness. So we decided to go a different route and design and build our own creatures." Faced with creating two essentially distinct creatures - the mogwai, as typified by Gizmo and his five cuddly offspring; and the gremlins, best characterized by the violently off-the-wall Stripe - Walas quickly found that designing the more menacing variant came easiest. "The gremlins, or GMs, were definitely the simplest to design. I found myself moving very quickly on that. The actual concept of the script had the gremlins as basically lizard-like. But between talks with Joe and Mike, we decided that lizards are lizards. They aren't scary, and they certainly aren't funny. So I tried to put a little more character into them. We knew that they were completely crazy little monsters, and we knew that we wanted to make them reptilian. But I also wanted them to look wild. So I gave them long arms and bony fingers; and I gave them big ears, because they're night creatures. There's a little suggestion in the GMs of bats. Then I gave them more of a face than a regular animal would have, because they have more character. To keep that animal look, I kept the head low, but I brought the face forward, almost to human proportions. Still, the predominant look was reptilian, so we went through many books on reptiles, picking out characteristics as we went along. I've always been a reptile fan, since I was a kid. In fact, I wanted, at one point, to be a herpitologist. So I've always been conscious of scale patterns and that sort of thing - which is why I incorporated overlapping scales on certain areas of the GMs that act like armor, beaded scaling around the face that varied a whole lot, texturally, and a nictating membrane in the eyelids. Unfortunately, you never really get a good look at those membranes in the film, except for a quick shot in Dorry's Tavern during the bar scene." In all, more than a hundred 'standard' gremlin puppets - twenty-three inches tall, with ten-inch bat ears-were constructed, featuring foam latex faces and urethane bodies covered with latex skin. Other, more specialized, versions were devised to perform specific functions. Though all were predominantly greenish-brown in color, the 'Stripe' puppets - of which there were fourteen different versions - were rendered more distinctive by a crowning 'punker' slash of dead-white fur. "While I'had had a lot of fun on the basic gremlin design," Walas continued, "the mogwai were another thing entirely. It took us seven months to nail that design down. With the mogwai, we were constantly fooling around and changing things, because it's very challenging to try and come up with something that Is basical a ted bei is basically a teddy bear but doesn't look like a teddy bear. The overriding idea, always, was that the mogwai be as cute as possible, and initially Chris Columbus had them looking like little hamsters. But gradually we grew away from that." The mogwai design began at its most basic - coloration. Steven Spielberg's dog Chauncey was ultimately responsible for this bit of detail, since Walas based the mogwai's tan-and-white markings on the director's pet. "The mogwai nose," said Walas, "was half-puppy, half-monkey - just your standard, cute, animal nose." About twenty full-bodied, ten-inch mogwai puppets were built, with a dozen of that number representing different versions of the Gizmo character. The standard mogwai were equipped with latex and urethane hands and feet and foam latex faces. "Putting hair on those small mogwai puppets was a problem. We couldn't get woven hair to behave well enough on netting, since the netting was so stiff that when it was stretched out over our interior mechanisms, it often restricted them and created awkward folds. We did a lot of tests with rubberizing fur, but there was just so much stress and work going on with these puppets that nothing held up very well except cloth backing. So we then had some specific synthetic fur run up for us by two companies - one on the east coast, one on the west. We were constantly rechecking that fur before every single shot - making sure the hair was brushed the right way, and that there weren't any dirty marks or tears in the foam. We also had to make sure that the mogwai's eyes and noses were always wet." For this purpose, a methycellulose mixture was found to be most effective. With the basic mogwai design at last agreed upon, one of the executive producers threw Walas an unexpected curve. "About two months before the beginning of production," said cinematographer John Hora,iSteven Spielberg had a brainstorm. Instead of having Gizmo change into the lead gremlin - which was in our script up to this point - Spielberg was going to have him remain a mogwai and help fight the gremlins and become a hero at the end. This threw Chris Walas and everybody else for a lurch, because they had made the mogwai so small that it was almost impossible to articulate the structure of their bodies. Their legs were so short that if they had taken a step, they would have fallen over. That had been okay, originally, because Gizmo was going to be there for only about a third of the film. But suddenly, he had to carry the show! It was obvious that with what little time we had left, Chris wasn't going to be able to come up with something sophisticated enough - especially with all the work he already had facing him. So Joe decided the best thing to do would be to stick Gizmo in a backpack or have somebody carry him in his arms whenever he needed to walk. That way he never had to." Of course, Walas did not labor alone. He was, in fact, aided by a preproduction crew of approximately two dozen coworkers - a team which swelled to forty during the actual shoot.Ethan Wiley was very important to me," said Walas. "Early on, he helped quite a bit in getting the mogwai mechanics together and keeping them straightened out, as did Gary Platek. Eben Stromquist designed most of the more elaborate mechanical devices, and Tim Gillette came in a little later and took over for Gary Platek." As for sculpting, Randy Dutra assumed such chores throughout preproduction and principal photography, with Anthony McVey assisting. "Actually, it was hard to

categorize most of the people on the Gremlins crew because I tried to give everybody a chance to change off and cross over with different responsibilities. That held true for the puppet operators as well. Surprisingly enough, a lot of the puppeteering requirements were specifically spatial. It was often just a matter of how big or how wide you were, and whether you could fit into and maintain the consistency of specific shots." Although many of the Gremlins puppet shots required fullbodied figures, there were numerous others where only one particular body segment would be in the frame. Accordingly, Walas and crew worked up a 'library' of mogwai and gremlin parts from literally hundreds of molds - a stockpile of limbs and such, always on call for any situation. Included among these spares were various bodies, heads, faces, tongues, eyes and The mogwai and gremlin parts were manufactured primarily at Walas' northern California facility, then shipped down to Los Angeles and assembled on-site in a 45-foot trailer designated as a mobile storage and workshop area for the team. "During principal photography," said Walas, "we used all sorts of methods to operate the mogwai and gremlins - radio signals, rods, handwork, marionetting, cables and what I call 'throw- 'em-across-the-room' puppetry. Whenever possible, though, we tried to use our cable operating system, since we felt we could get better results in subtleties of control. In conjunction with this, Gary Platek came up with a very versatile, very adaptable quick-change hand control system that worked out exceptionally well. They attached and detached in a few minutes, and were only about the size of a book. They really bypassed the standard levers used in cable control systems, which are usually about three feet tall and lined up side by side in clusters of two or four levers apiece - which takes up a lot of space. To first practice the creature movements, we'd all stand in front of a mirror and do little performances, just to get the basics of puppeteering down. Once we had a smooth consistency of movement, then we went for the little character traits." With the Gremlins puppet construction well in hand, Joe Dante's thoughts turned to visuals. His previous two outings - The Howling and "It's a Good Life" - had been highly stylized, due in no small part to John Hora's lurid color effects, constantly moving camera and odd, tilted angles which brought a near-expressionistic surface to both films. Gremlins was to be presented no differently. Dante's intent was to invest the film with not only the spirit of Chuck Jones and Tex Avery cartoons, but also with the anima of the late Italian horror director Mario Bava, an assured stylist whose often sadistic films clearly - at least in the visual sense - represent a spiritual kinship with Dante's later works. "Given the material of Gremlins," Dante said, "it seemed to me that the audience would be faced by a story which, even at the beginning - before anything really happened - would confront them with this absolutely fantastic set of circumstances. And the audience has to buy this set of circumstances in order to like the picture. So 12 - CINEFEX 19

it seemed to me that if Gremlins wasn't treated like a cartoon - or at least like a dream - then people were going to start asking all the wrong questions. And this is not a movie where you are supposed to ask questions." Rejecting any thought of employing actual locations and interiors, Dante immediately opted to film Gremlins under the most rigorously controlled of environments - studio soundstages and backlots. The decision was prompted not only by the obviously greater degree of control Walas would be allowed over his creature operations, but was also an extension of Dante's 'Gremlins as cartoon' philosophy. Shooting on a studio lot was absolutely a conscious decision," Dante commented. '¿From my point of view, I just felt that this story would not have worked if there had been any feeling of being out in a real town, of having real garbage trucks driving back and forth on real snow. The idea was to try and create a separate world that this picture could take place in - its own world, a place that would live by its own logic and its own set of rules. It was almost like making a film set on another planet. I guess Gremlins was really set in the world of remembered moviesi Not the least of these remembered movies was Frank Capra's perennial favorite, It's a Wonderful Life - with Gremlins' Kingston Falls a conscious evocation of the earlier film's Bedford Falls locale. The bulk of the Gremlins interiors were shot at The Burbank Studios," explained Mike Finnell. "We were also going to shoot the Kingston Falls main street and town square locations there - on what's known as the Dukes of Hazard street - but there were some scheduling problems, so we moved across to Universal and used their town square set for those shots." The exterior of the Kingston Falls YMCA was shot at Universal, but the swimming pool within was actually an exterior pool - rigged with two walls standing open to the air - a pool located at the Columbia Ranch, where the exteriors of the Peltzer and Futterman homes were also photographed. Only the sheriff's office sequences were shot on a non-studio location, during a two-day stint at Washington High School in nearby Pasadena. Principal photography began officially on April 27, 1983. To open the film, Dante had decided to treat his audience with a return to the old Warner Brothers logo that had graced the majority of that studio's releases until the 1970s, when Saul Bass' 'worm logo' (so called because its stylized 'W' looked as though it were made out of worms) became the studio's new trademark. Securing the vintage logo for Gremlins was no simple matter, however. "We were pumping for the old Warners logo," said Dante, because we just felt that we didn't want to use the worm logo. It's a fine trademark, but it's not for the Warner Brothers that / remember. So we started badgering the studio about using the old logo; and at about the same time, Swing Shift, which was also ready to come out, wanted to use the old logo as well. Finally, the combined weight of both of these pictures managed to get Warners to make up a new 'old' logo. Then I talked Jerry Goldsmith into redoing the old Max Steiner fanfare. While we were all being very thrilled by this, Warner Brothers suddenly decided to adopt this logo for all its pictures. And one of the first places they dumped it was onto The Neverending Story trailer, which went out to theaters all over the country affixed to the head of the first reel of our Gremlins prints. So all the fun of going to the movie and suddenly seeing the old Warner Brothers logo come on with the old music was vitiated by the fact that it had already appeared five minutes earlier in front of this trailer." Gremlins opens with inventor Rand Peltzer (Hoyt Axton) prowling the smoky, neon-lit backstreets of an unnamed Chinatown in search of an unusual Christmas present for his son Billy (Zach Galligan). Though the Burbank Studios' time-worn 'tenement street' - recently rebuilt for Annie - was a handsome standin for a true Chinatown locale, the sequence was not without its detractors. "In the literal-minded production meetings we were having," said Dante, "I was forever being asked: 'Where is this Chinatown? San Francisco? Hong Kong? Where?' Actually, in the first drafts of the script, it's specified that Rand is flying home from Hong Kong. Well, then we were asked: 'If this guy is an unsuccessful inventor who is living off his son's salary at the town bank, where does he get the money to fly to Hong Kong to try and sell his dumb products? And how do you get a mogwai through customs?' So we got very nonspecific, and I just kept saying, 'It's Chinatown at Warner Brothers!' Luckily, when people watch the movie, they tend to take Chinatown as a state of mind rather than a real place.i At one point, Dante had planned to replace the Chinatown sequence with one in which Gizmo is discovered in a Texas desert at a rundown roadside gift and curio shop, but the more exotic locale ultimately Following a Chinese boy to the curio shop of his grandfather (Keye Luke), Peltzer is soon drawn to soft singing coming from a dark corner of the old man's establishment. "This, of course, is where Peltzer first encounters Gizmo," said John Hora, "but you don't see him yet. You also don't see a lot of the props in that shop in the final cut. We really had that place dressed to the rafters. Skulls, paintings, books, oriental masks, a chessboard of demons and gargoyles - everything that seemed occult-ish was in there." One detail on quite visible display, however, is Luke's black and gold blind eye - a contact lens effect courtesy of opthamologist Morton Greenspoon, a frequent supplier of specialized lenses for Hollywood productions. Across the Eighth Dimension with Buckaroo Banzai

Any film that strives to depict the eighth dimension, an invisible tenth planet, spaceships that look like seashells and interdimensional aliens who are all named John demands total suspension of disbelief. And the extent to which The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai is successful in this regard can be laid, in part, upon the artistry and technological know-how of the people who labored on its special effects. In all, three companies were principally engaged in the effects effort. Dream Quest Images produced approximately thirty shots involving miniature spaceships, matte paintings and some optical compositing. Peter Kuran and VCE, Inc., were responsible for another sixty-four effects shots, including all the live-action bluescreen work, various animation effects and more optical compositing, Finally, John Scheele and Greenlite Effects, Inc., tackled the brief but interesting segment in the eighth dimension. Because of its original design - and in some cases, equally unusual execution - Buckaroo Banzai strained the boundaries of the known. After all, no one knew what the eighth dimension should look like; no one knew what an alien Lectroid should look like; and certainly, no one knew how to make a seashell fly. Even so, first-time director W.D. Richter never thought of Buckaroo Banzai as a special effects film. "Our approach was not to have the movie hang on special effects-not to give one effect after the other. Our effects punctuate a human story, and so we didn't feel we had to try and top such films as Star Wars and Return of the Jedi. We tried to be original in our design." Taking their cue from nature rather than high technology, Richter and production designer Michael Riva designed spaceships, aliens and 'other worlds' that have few precedents in film. Richter encouraged input from everybody on the show, and as in all good science fiction, origins were established for the worlds involved. "We decided from the start that the whole movie was going to have a production design that was ramshackle or pasted together, as the real world is," said Richter. "It wouldn't be slick and it wouldn't look like it had been stamped out by a Hollywood studio. Factories and military facilities and houses really look messy - which to us said 'organic.' It's a lived-in, cluttered world. So when it came time to design the spaceships, that word 'organic' kept coming up. We were not going to do things with wings and conventional cockpits in them. We were going to take that notion of 'organic' into nature and see what we got back. As a result, some of the early designs were as simple as eucalyptus pods that fall off trees and are spiky and strange. In the opening moments of Dreamscape, a lone woman runs for her life down an empty highway as the New York skyline stands surreally behind her. Suddenly, a blinding light flashes out, causing the city to erupt in a mushroom cloud of destruction. One second more, and the woman is blasted by a wave of brilliant light and searing heat. These are the elements of a recurring nightmare which, for the President of the United States, has a special meaning because the woman is his wife. For his enemies, however, it signifies something else - a weakness that cannot be tolerated. When they seek to kill him by invading this realm of the subconscious, the President's nightmare takes on yet a different significance for a young psychic named Alex Gardner. For him, it becomes the bizarre backdrop for a desperate battle beyond the world of the conscious in ... the dreamscape. For special visual and makeup effects artists Peter Kuran, Craig Reardon and James Aupperle, this nightmare and the many others in Dreamscape proved to mean something else - the opportunity to create the effects for an $8 million production. Prior to Dreamscape, all three had separately been involved with a wide variety of movies, from the Star Wars trilogy to Poltergeist and Caveman. Now they would join forces to create the surreal visions required for Dreamscape. As with any film, however, before they were through they would find themselves caught up in another realm of the unknown - the sometimes nightmarish world of film production. Dreamscape stars Dennis Quaid as Alex, a gifted psychic who becomes involved in a series of experiments in dream participation. Using his extrasensory abilities, Alex soon learns to project himself into other people's dreams for the purpose of altering those dreams and relieving the subconscious trauma at their root. First, the actors were filmed on a full-size trolley set against a blue screen. Though quite detailed, the models were not very large. The biggest, in fact - the Capitol in ruins - was only about two-and-a-half feet tall, and the rest of the devastated buildings ranged in sizes smaller than that to diminish the perspective. "We filmed the miniatures against the second blue screen," said Kuran, "so that I would have the ability to put in a sky and buildings on the horizon that were much smaller than the ones in the foreground. The first would be an accurate representation of actor David Patrick Kelly, scaled down to about five inches in height. From this, a casting would be made which would be built up slightly with clay. Unfortunately, because of time, Reardon decided to alter his planned approach slightly. "When I realized my time problem, I decided I couldn't wait to make a mold of each stage before going on to the next step. Making a good mold and cast can take up to twenty-four hours, and I didn't think I would have enough time to wait for that, especially if I had to wait in between each of the proposed fortyeight heads. So instead, I decided to make thirty-two copies of the actor's face, alter the first one slightly, then step over to the next, match it to the one before and then build up on it a little more, step over to the next and match it with the previous one and then build up on it a little more, until I reached the final head. That proved to be a big mistake because it took so much time to match by eye each of those subtle changes, and it meant literally resculpting the previous head from scratch before I could go on and add the next stage. I used calipers when I could, but mainly I ended up trying to match by eye. The result was some slight anomalies between each change, which caused slight tremulations or jerkiness. By the time I was finished with the whole series of heads, the producer was a little alarmed that there were these palpitations. I was disappointed by that - not because of the quality of the dissolves, which were great - but because my goal had been to avoid them. In addition to the work done by Kuran, Reardon and Aupperle, Dreamscape features some supplemental footage contributed by independent filmmaker Dennis Pies. With the exception of the opening nightmare, all of the dream sequences in the film begin with a strange journey through a tunnel-like realm of special effects that brings to mind the opening of the old Twilight Zone TV series. When Kuran considered how such effects should be done, he recalled a film by Pies that he had seen as a student at the California School of the Arts. At that time, Kuran had been impressed by the film's dreamlike quality and its unusual effects sequences. Locating a print of the film, Kuran showed it to Dreamscape producer Bruce Cohn Curtis, who also liked the images and agreed that Pies could provide the look they wanted. Kuran then initiated a search for the filmmaker, found him teaching courses at Harvard, and asked him to join the project. Working in a studio at Harvard, Pies created the tunnel effects by photographing various chemicals in layers on an Oxberry animation stand. To this footage, Kuran added shots of sparkle dust filmed against black, and modified some of Pies' work optically to suggest different moods and looks for each individual dream. For Kuran, Reardon and Aupperle, Dreamscape was an experience involving a wide variety of problems that had to be solved quickly and inexpensively. From the nuclear nightmare that opens the film to the final battle with the Tommy Ray snakeman, it was an adventure not only into the realm of the dreamscape, but also into the world of low-budget effects productions. "We all just had to sort of sweat and figure out ways of doing the effects that looked interesting and off-the-wall," Kuran reflected, but that wouldn't require sophisticated or expensive equipment. Most of the visual effects in the film were created without very sophisticated equipment - the most complex piece used on the film was probably my optical printer. We didn't use motion control, nothing. It was all sort of hand-done, off-the-wall stuff that came together to become what it was. Dreamscape was definitely one of the lowest-tech movies ever made; but in the end, I think we're all proud of our work, even if it wasn't always as wild and refined as we would have liked."
